item.title: Network tiers
item.description:
Every VM goes through a proxy that devvm runs for it on this machine, and the VM’s network tier decides what the proxy lets it reach. New VMs get the allowlist tier by default, so they reach only the hosts on their allowlist. No VM holds your secrets, whatever its tier, because its proxy puts them into its requests. A secret is a credential devvm keeps on this machine for VMs to use: your GitHub token, Claude Code’s token, an agent’s login or an API key. An open VM, the one tier that isn’t confined to its proxy, reaches anything this machine can, including this machine’s own services on localhost and your LAN.

sequenceDiagram
participant P as The VM
participant X as Its proxy,<br>on this machine
participant H as api.github.com
P->>X: GET /user, with<br>a placeholder
Note over X: on the allowlist
X->>H: GET /user, with<br>your GitHub token
H-->>X: the response
X-->>P: the response
P->>X: CONNECT<br>example.com:443
X-->>P: 403: not on<br>the allowlist

This page covers what you do with a VM’s tier and what you see. How it works › Network tiers explains how devvm confines a VM to its proxy and how the proxy handles each connection.

Network tiers

A VM is on one of four tiers, from the lowest to the highest:

Tier What the VM reaches Confined to its proxy
open whatever this machine reaches, its localhost and the LAN included; the proxy applies no rules no
internet every public host, on any port, apart from your denies; never this machine’s addresses or its networks' yes
allowlist only the hosts its allowlists allow, apart from your denies yes
none only its agents’ hosts, the hosts of its secrets and logins, and its links, apart from your denies yes

--network TIER chooses a new VM’s tier, and devvm network with a tier changes an existing VM’s, such as devvm network internet (choosing a tier). A higher tier is stricter, and a VM on any tier but open is confined: it reaches nothing but its proxy, and a direct connection from it fails.

An open VM runs on its backend’s own network, so it reaches this machine and your LAN directly, as a VM without a proxy would. Its environment names its proxy all the same (HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY and their lowercase forms), and the proxy reaches every host and address for it, this machine’s localhost and your LAN included, so a tool behaves the same through the proxy as it does directly. Its NO_PROXY names the VM itself and this machine as the VM reaches it, host.lima.internal, so requests to those go directly. Every launch checks that an open VM’s proxy is set in the VM and answers it, and when it doesn’t, devvm warns you and opens the VM all the same. An open VM gets a placeholder for each secret it may use, as every VM does, and only its proxy puts the real value in. So a request that goes around the proxy, directly from the VM, carries only the placeholder, and the secret’s host refuses it.

On the internet and none tiers, devvm reads only the denies of your policy files: the internet tier allows every public host itself, and the none tier allows only what the VM’s agents, secrets and links need. devvm network marks each such file (denies only), and when you add an allow to a VM on either tier, devvm says that the allow changes nothing until the VM is on the allowlist tier. On the open tier no rule applies at all.

Changing a VM from one confined tier to another applies at once, because the VM’s proxy starts again with the new tier’s rules and the VM keeps running. A change into or out of the open tier applies from the VM’s next start, as below describes. devvm ls and devvm network show a VM’s tier, or unenforced when a confined tier isn’t in force (when it isn’t enforced).

Choosing a tier

A new VM gets the allowlist tier unless you choose another, and the summary devvm shows before it makes the VM names its tier. When you customize the VM in a terminal, devvm lists the four tiers, each with what it reaches, and the tier the summary showed is chosen (what a new VM gets):

Network tier for devvm-some-project-71a99b1076d92c (up/down to choose, enter to confirm):
 ( ) open reaches anything this machine can
 ( ) internet reaches any public host
> (*) allowlist reaches only the hosts you allow (recommended)
 ( ) none reaches only its agents' and secrets' hosts and its links

Up and down move the choice, and enter gives the VM the chosen tier, so pressing enter at once keeps the tier the summary showed. --network TIER answers the question up front, such as devvm --network internet, and when there’s no terminal to ask in, or you give --no-input, the VM gets the tier the summary showed. A VM keeps its tier. On an existing VM devvm ignores --network and warns you, naming the devvm network command that changes the tier.

To give every new VM another tier, save it with devvm network -g, such as devvm network -g none, or choose it in devvm setup. Each new VM’s summary then shows that tier, and customizing the VM still asks, with Enter keeping the saved tier. devvm network -g shows what new VMs get, allowlist until you save another tier, followed by where it came from after a #, and devvm network -g --json prints it as policy, with source. devvm reads the saved tier only when it creates a VM, so the VMs you already have keep their own tier, and --network still chooses for one new VM. You can also set it with network in config.toml, which wins over the saved tier, and then devvm network -g refuses to change it and names the file (where a default comes from).

Lima confines every VM to its proxy, so every VM can be on any tier, the docker layer’s included. devvm never starts a VM on a confined tier with an open network, so if a VM’s backend couldn’t confine it, the VM could only be open: devvm would refuse to make it on any other tier unless you give --network open, and it would refuse to give it any other tier with devvm network (when a backend lacks something).
devvm network print this folder’s VM’s tier as devvm ls shows it, open, internet, allowlist, none or unenforced, and then its allowlist
devvm network open|internet|allowlist|none change it: between confined tiers at once, and into or out of open from the VM’s next start, which devvm restart gives you, and for a running VM, ask in a terminal whether to restart it now
devvm network -g [open|internet|allowlist|none] show or change what new VMs get

When a change into or out of open finds the VM running, devvm asks in a terminal whether to restart it now, which stops anything running in it, and if you answer yes, it restarts the VM as devvm restart does, so the change applies at once. If you answer no, or there’s no terminal, or you pass --no-input, the change waits until the VM starts again. If you give a running open VM a confined tier, the VM isn’t confined yet, so devvm ls shows it as unenforced, and its next launch offers to restart it confined, as it does for a VM started outside devvm. If you make a VM open while it runs confined, its launches keep it confined to its proxy, which now applies an open VM’s rules, until it next starts, and they warn you that the VM leaves its proxy’s confinement when it next starts. In a terminal, each of those launches first asks whether to restart the VM now, with no as the default unless an agent’s new folders wait too (restarting).

When it isn’t enforced

On every launch devvm checks on this machine that the VM still runs on the process devvm started confined, and that a direct connection from the VM to the internet fails. A VM that fails either check shows as unenforced, and devvm offers to restart it confined or stops it, as the self-check describes.

Allowlists

The VM’s proxy reads devvm’s built-in policies first and then your policy files, in order, as one list:

  • devvm’s own rules for every VM, which allow OS packages, mise’s version lists, the Sigstore and GitHub trust roots that mise checks a download’s attestations against, Node’s downloads for a project’s own node, and GitHub;
  • devvm’s rules for each shared tool in the VM’s image (node, claude and the others), which allow its registries, downloads and APIs;
  • devvm’s rules for each built-in layer in the VM’s image, so the docker layer allows Docker’s packages and the container registries Docker Hub and ghcr.io, and the nix layer allows Nix’s binary cache, channels and flake registry;
  • ~/.config/devvm/layers/<name>.policy, for each of your own layers in the VM’s image;
  • ~/.config/devvm/policy, your own rules for every VM, which devvm network allow, deny and rm change with -g;
  • ~/.local/share/devvm/vms/<hash>/policy, the rules for that VM only, in the VM’s own folder, which is named by the hash that the VM’s name ends with, which devvm network allow, deny and rm change;
  • the hosts of the VM’s secrets and logins, and the host its agents log in at, such as Codex’s and opencode’s auth.openai.com and Claude Code’s platform.claude.com and console.anthropic.com, on port 443, which devvm adds.

The first three are built in: they come with devvm, inside its binary, so you can’t edit them, and an upgrade of devvm is what changes them. To change what a VM reaches, add your own rules, and to keep a VM from a host that devvm’s rules allow, add a deny, which beats any allow. devvm leaves storage and paste sites out of its defaults on purpose, because they’re easy ways to send data out. Rules never come from the project folder, because the VM can write it. The proxy reads each of your files again when it changes, so an edit applies at once, from the next connection. How it works lists where each policy comes from.

Rules

A policy file holds one rule per line. # starts a comment, and matching ignores case.

Rule Matches
example.com that host only
*.example.com any subdomain, at any depth, not example.com itself
** any host, and any address, though an internal address still needs its own rule
10.0.0.5, 10.0.0.0/8, fd00::/8 addresses, IPv4 or IPv6 (also what lets a connection past the internal-address refusal)
RULE:22, [fd00::1]:22, 10.0.0.0/8:8080 only that port; without a port, 443 and 80
RULE:*, **:* any port
!RULE deny: a deny beats any allow

A rule is plain ASCII with no spaces in it, and a port is a number from 1 to 65535, or * for any port. A host’s one trailing dot is dropped, so example.com. matches example.com. Brackets hold only an IPv6 address, and an address can’t follow *.. A line that holds anything else, such as example.com:x, a*.example.com or ! example.com with a space after the !, isn’t a rule.

When a line that isn’t a rule starts with !, it reads as a deny, but the proxy can’t tell what it would deny. So while the line is there, the proxy of every VM that reads the file denies every new connection apart from the VM’s links, whatever the other rules allow. Connections that are already open stay open. Each refusal names the file and the line, and it suggests no devvm network allow command, because no rule would help. Any other line that isn’t a rule is skipped, and the file’s other lines still apply. The proxy names each such line in its own log.

devvm warns about each line that isn’t a rule, with the file and the line’s number, and the warning for a broken deny says that the proxies deny everything until it’s fixed. It warns when you open a confined VM whose proxy reads the file, when devvm network allow, deny or rm changes the file, and in devvm doctor. devvm network also marks the line. Fix the line or remove it, and the change applies from the next connection.

The proxy never dials a denied address, even for an allowed name that resolves to it or to its NAT64 form. A missing file has no rules. A file that changed but can’t be read keeps its last rules, so a deny never lapses.

Changing rules

devvm network shows this folder’s VM’s allowlist after its tier. It prints each of the VM’s policies that holds more than comments, and then its rules without their comments. A built-in policy has its name after # devvm:, because it has no file you could edit, and one of your files has its path after #, followed by (denies only) on the internet and none tiers, where it shows only the file’s denies. An open VM has no policies, so devvm network prints its tier alone. A line that isn’t a rule is marked # not a rule, skipped, with its line number:

allowlist
# devvm: layers/base.policy
 ports.ubuntu.com
 github.com
# /Users/you/.local/share/devvm/vms/71a99b1076d92c/policy
 example.com
 example.com:x # not a rule, skipped (line 2)
devvm network allow RULE... add the rules to the VM’s own file
devvm network deny RULE... add them as denies, adding ! when it’s missing
devvm network rm RULE... remove the lines with these rules, a deny with its !, and warn about one that isn’t there
-g, --global with allow, deny or rm, change ~/.config/devvm/policy, for every VM, instead, which needs no VM

A rule is what Rules lists, without spaces or a comment. devvm refuses anything else before it adds any rule, and it also refuses allow !RULE. A rule that’s already in the file, in any case, isn’t added again. Each change applies at once, from the next connection. For an open VM, devvm notes that no rule applies to it, and for an allow on the internet or none tier, that only denies apply there. When devvm network log --blocked or a blocked request in the VM suggests a devvm network allow command, its rule is one that devvm network allow takes.

If a VM was deleted outside devvm, devvm deletes what it kept for that VM when it makes a new VM for the same project folder, so the new VM never gets the old one’s rules.

devvm network –json

devvm network --json prints the VM’s tier and its allowlist as one JSON object, as output for scripts describes. policy is open, internet, allowlist, none or unenforced, and allowlist has each policy that holds more than comments, in the order the proxy reads them. Each has builtin, a built-in policy’s name, or file, the path of one of your files, then its rules and, in not_rules, each line that isn’t a rule, with its line number and its text. On the internet and none tiers, a file whose denies alone apply also has denies_only set to true, and its rules are its denies, as devvm network lists them under (denies only). Without denies_only, a file’s rules are all of its rules. With -g, the object has only policy, which is the tier new VMs get, and source, which says where it came from: config.toml, settings.json for what devvm network -g or devvm setup saved, or built-in (where a default comes from). With --json the command only shows, so devvm refuses a tier with it.

{
 "version": 1,
 "policy": "allowlist",
 "source": "config.toml"
}
{
 "version": 1,
 "policy": "allowlist",
 "allowlist": [
 {
 "builtin": "layers/base.policy",
 "rules": [
 "ports.ubuntu.com",
 "github.com"
 ],
 "not_rules": []
 },
 {
 "file": "/Users/you/.local/share/devvm/vms/71a99b1076d92c/policy",
 "rules": [
 "example.com"
 ],
 "not_rules": [
 {
 "line": 2,
 "text": "example.com:x"
 }
 ]
 }
 ]
}

On the none tier, a VM with Claude Code gets Claude Code’s built-in policy whole, and its own file shows only its denies:

{
 "version": 1,
 "policy": "none",
 "allowlist": [
 {
 "builtin": "shared-tools/claude.policy",
 "rules": [
 "api.anthropic.com",
 "claude.ai"
 ],
 "not_rules": []
 },
 {
 "file": "/Users/you/.local/share/devvm/vms/71a99b1076d92c/policy",
 "denies_only": true,
 "rules": [
 "!tracker.example.com"
 ],
 "not_rules": []
 }
 ]
}

Inside the VM

Every login in the VM has the proxy settings in its environment (HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY and their lowercase forms, NO_PROXY for the VM itself, and NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY), and the CA variables that every VM has point the tools that don’t read the system’s store at the VM’s own CAs. devvm also points apt, sudo, ssh and Docker at the proxy (how), on every tier. On a confined tier, a direct connection fails at once, even as root, and so does DNS, because names resolve in the proxy. A tool that skips the proxy, even for a host the rules allow, fails with a DNS or connection error rather than the proxy’s 403, and nothing reaches the log (what to do).

A blocked request gets 403, and the response names the host, the reason and the rule that would allow it. The proxy also answers at http://devvm.proxy/:

  • /blocked lists the last 50 blocks.
  • /blocked/new?after=N gives the number of blocks so far, then those after the Nth, with each rule once, so a shell prompt can show what a command hit.
  • /ca.pem is the VM’s own CA certificate and the next one’s, never their keys.
  • /nix/ is the shared Nix cache, in a VM with the nix layer (below).

In the VM, devvm-why prints what the proxy blocked lately, and a note before each prompt tells you when something new was blocked. When the proxy blocked nothing lately, devvm-why says so, and it adds that a DNS or connection error for a host the tier allows means the tool skipped the proxy, so you turn on the tool’s own proxy setting or give it the address in $HTTPS_PROXY (a host on the allowlist doesn’t resolve). devvm also tells Claude Code and Codex, in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md and ~/.codex/AGENTS.md, why a request may fail and to run devvm-why, and that such an error while devvm-why shows nothing means the tool skipped the proxy.

Nix

In a VM with the nix layer, Nix’s daemon makes most of Nix’s downloads, and devvm also points it at the proxy, so its downloads go through the same allowlists. The layer’s allowlist has cache.nixos.org for Nix’s binary cache, and channels.nixos.org and releases.nixos.org for its channels and flake registry, and GitHub, where most flakes’ inputs come from, is in devvm’s rules for every VM.

Nix asks the proxy’s shared cache, http://devvm.proxy/nix, before cache.nixos.org, so every VM with the layer shares the packages that any of them downloaded (shared downloads). The proxy fetches what the cache doesn’t have from cache.nixos.org alone, and only while the VM’s tier and rules let it reach cache.nixos.org. It keeps a package only when cache.nixos.org’s signature on it checks, and the VM’s Nix checks that signature again. A VM can only make the proxy fetch from cache.nixos.org: the proxy refuses anything a VM sends to store, and every request that isn’t for one of Nix’s cache files. Each request shows in devvm network log as cache, with whether it was a hit, fetched, or why it wasn’t found. What one VM can learn of another through the cache is under Attack vectors. An open VM has its proxy too, so it shares the cache as well, and its proxy fetches from cache.nixos.org for it.

When a package isn’t in the binary cache, Nix builds it from source, and the build downloads its sources from their own hosts, such as ftpmirror.gnu.org. The proxy blocks those hosts until you allow them, so the build fails, and the error, devvm-why and devvm network log --blocked name the host and the devvm network allow command that allows it.

Behind a company proxy

When this machine reaches the internet only through a company proxy, the VM’s proxy sends the requests it allows through that proxy. devvm reads HTTPS_PROXY, HTTP_PROXY and NO_PROXY, or their lowercase forms, from the shell you run it in. When that shell sets neither HTTPS_PROXY nor HTTP_PROXY, devvm reads the [proxy] table of config.toml instead, so the proxy works from every shell, including an editor’s terminal that didn’t load your profile. The shell’s settings win whole: devvm never mixes them with config.toml’s, so a NO_PROXY alone in the shell still leaves config.toml’s proxy in effect, with its own no-proxy.

[proxy]
https = "http://alice@proxy.example.com:8080"
http = "http://alice@proxy.example.com:8080"
no-proxy = "localhost,.example.com"

devvm passes the settings to the VM’s proxy when the proxy starts, and when you run devvm again with different settings, devvm starts the VM’s proxy again with the new ones. So after you change them, run devvm again in the folder or devvm restart. When a VM’s proxy went through a company proxy the last time it started and devvm finds none this time, devvm warns you and names config.toml, because a VM’s proxy that a shell without the settings starts sends the VM’s requests directly.

The VM’s proxy still decides each request by the host name the VM asked for, against the same allowlists, and only then passes it on. It sends tunnels, which carry HTTPS and the requests it puts your secrets into, through HTTPS_PROXY’s proxy, and plain HTTP requests through HTTP_PROXY’s. It reaches the hosts that NO_PROXY names directly, and also localhost and loopback addresses. In NO_PROXY, example.com matches that host and its subdomains, .example.com matches only its subdomains, an address or a CIDR matches addresses, any entry can end in a port, and * matches every host. devvm network log adds through host:port to each request that went through the company proxy.

The company proxy needs an http:// address, such as http://user:password@proxy.example.com:8080 in HTTPS_PROXY, and a proxy without a port is on port 80. devvm doesn’t start a VM’s proxy while HTTPS_PROXY, HTTP_PROXY or a [proxy] key names an https:// or socks5:// proxy, and it tells you which setting to change. The company proxy’s password stays on this machine. The VM never gets it, and devvm writes it into no log, no image and no process’s arguments.

config.toml never holds the password, because it’s a file you might copy to other machines or keep with your dotfiles, and devvm refuses a [proxy] URL that has one. Put only the user in the URL, as http://alice@proxy.example.com:8080, and save the password with devvm secret set proxy, which keeps it as it keeps the other secrets. devvm’s proxies look it up themselves when they start, so no file of devvm’s holds it in the clear. devvm doesn’t make a new VM, start a VM’s proxy, or build an image or the shared tools while config.toml’s proxy names a user and no password is saved, and it checks before anything starts. A VM’s proxy reads the password only when it starts, so after you change it, run devvm restart in each VM’s folder. No VM ever gets the proxy secret, and devvm secret use proxy refuses.

The company proxy sees the name and port of every host the VM reaches, and if it inspects TLS, the CA you add for it also lets it read the traffic. The company proxy also looks up each name itself, so the VM’s proxy can’t check every address a name leads to. It still refuses an address that’s this machine’s own or internal, unless a rule names it, and it refuses a name when this machine’s lookup gives an internal or denied address for it. A name that this machine can’t look up goes to the company proxy unchecked only when an allowlist names it, as example.com or *.example.com. When only ** allows a name that this machine can’t look up, the VM’s proxy refuses it, so ** never lets a VM send the company proxy a name of its own making. What a VM can still reach through the company proxy, such as hosts on your company’s network, is under Attack vectors.

Open VMs and builds

An open VM goes through its proxy as every VM does, and its proxy sends its requests through the company proxy, from the shell’s settings or config.toml’s, so the company proxy’s password stays on this machine for it too. The VM never gets the shell’s proxy settings, and Lima gets none to pass on to it. What an open VM reaches directly, past its proxy, such as the hosts its NO_PROXY names, doesn’t go through the company proxy.

Lima prints each proxy setting it gives a VM, password and all, as it starts the VM. devvm keeps the password out of its run log, and once the VM has started, it replaces the password with as many * in the log Lima keeps for the VM.

Builds never get your company proxy’s settings, and images never keep them. A build goes through the shell’s company proxy, or else config.toml’s, as a VM’s proxy does. When devvm builds an image, builds the shared tools or converts a --from container image on Lima behind a company proxy, the build goes through a proxy of devvm’s on this machine, made for that build alone, which goes through your company proxy. The build’s commands get only that proxy’s address, with a password devvm makes for the build, while they run, and devvm stops the proxy when the build ends. So the code a build runs, which includes a container image’s own, never sees your company proxy’s address or password. That proxy also runs on this machine, so a company proxy on localhost, such as one a VPN client runs, works for builds too.

A build’s proxy allows any host, as ** does. It sends a name that this machine can’t look up on to the company proxy, so builds work where only the company proxy looks up outside names.

devvm’s own downloads on this machine go through the company proxy too. They are devvm’s copy of mise and the versions it looks up for the shared tools, the list of Ubuntu’s cloud images, and a container registry’s answers for --from. With the shell’s settings, each of them uses the shell’s. With config.toml’s, devvm’s own requests send the password only to the company proxy. The mise it runs on this machine gets the proxy’s URL with the password in it, in its environment, because mise takes a proxy’s password nowhere else. devvm percent-encodes the password in that URL and mise decodes it before it sends it, so a password with characters such as @, :, /, #, % or a space works too. devvm never puts that URL in mise’s arguments or in a file. When a VM’s proxy refreshes a Codex or opencode login on this machine, the refresh goes through the same company proxy as the VM’s requests, with the password kept on this machine.

Tools that ignore the proxy

On the open tier, a tool that ignores the proxy settings in the VM’s environment connects directly, past its proxy. Its connections still work, because an open VM reaches everything this machine can, but they don’t show in devvm network log, they don’t go through your company proxy, and a request of theirs that needs one of your secrets carries only its placeholder, so the secret’s host refuses it. On every other tier such a tool’s direct connection fails, so it needs the proxy’s address in its own settings. These common tools don’t read HTTP_PROXY and HTTPS_PROXY, or read them only when told to:

  • Node’s fetch reads them only with NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1, from Node 24.0.0 and 22.21.0, or with --use-env-proxy, from Node 24.5.0 and 22.21.0. devvm sets NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY in every VM, so an older Node’s fetch is the one that connects directly.
  • Python’s aiohttp reads them only when a program makes its session with trust_env=True.
  • Go programs read them through Go’s default HTTP transport, but a program that makes its own transport without a proxy function connects directly.
  • Java reads none of them. It takes its proxy from the https.proxyHost and https.proxyPort system properties, such as -Dhttps.proxyHost=…, and http.proxyHost and http.proxyPort for plain HTTP.
  • The Docker daemon reads them only from its own environment as it starts, or from its daemon.json, never from your shell. devvm points the daemon at the proxy itself, as Inside the VM says.

Secrets

Secrets stay on this machine, whatever the VM’s tier. A VM gets a placeholder of its own for each one, and its proxy puts the real value into requests for that secret’s hosts. An open VM can send a request around its proxy, but then the request carries only the placeholder, which the secret’s host refuses (tools that ignore the proxy). The proxy puts each secret into one header:

Secret Hosts Header Used by
claude api.anthropic.com Authorization every VM whose image has claude
github api.github.com, github.com, codeload.github.com, raw.githubusercontent.com Authorization VMs it’s bound to

Agents’ logins work the same way. When a VM’s image has a coding agent and devvm’s agent store has a login or an API key for it, the VM gets placeholders for the login, and so do Claude Code’s MCP servers’ secrets (agents’ logins and settings). A Claude Code, Codex or opencode login that you make inside a VM goes to the store, and the VM gets placeholders for it too (Claude Code login). A VM saves a login only for an agent that its image has, and its proxy refuses a login for any other agent, so a VM without Codex can never replace the store’s Codex login. Because the store keeps one login for each agent, any VM with the agent can replace it, so a VM you don’t trust can log your other VMs in to an account of its choosing (logins made in a VM).

Saving and binding secrets

Command What it does
devvm secret set claude or github asks for the Claude Code token or the GitHub token without showing it, and saves it (--stdin reads a line instead)
devvm secret set proxy asks for the company proxy’s password, for the user that config.toml’s [proxy] names, and saves it (--stdin reads a line instead)
devvm secret rm NAME deletes a saved secret
devvm secret lists the secrets, whether each is saved, and the VMs using each
devvm secret use NAME lets this folder’s VM use the secret
devvm secret unuse NAME stops this folder’s VM using it, though a VM whose image has claude always uses claude

devvm saves a secret in the macOS Keychain, or elsewhere in ~/.local/share/devvm/secrets/<name>, a file only you can read (details). No devvm command prints a saved secret, because each VM’s proxy reads the values it needs itself. devvm drops whitespace in a secret’s value, except inside the proxy password, which loses only the whitespace around it. It refuses a value with a quote, a backslash or a control character, and a claude value that isn’t a setup token (sk-ant-oat01-…, from claude setup-token). A CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN in devvm’s environment wins over a saved one.

Saving, deleting, binding and unbinding apply at once to the proxies that are running. From its next launch, the VM gets the placeholder in CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN or GH_TOKEN, and with github a git credential helper for https://github.com.

To put a secret in, the proxy shows the VM a certificate from the VM’s own CA, which every VM has, an open one’s included, and which no other VM trusts, so one VM’s proxy can’t make certificates that another VM accepts. Each CA lasts 30 days, and its key stays on this machine. Each launch installs the VM’s current CA and the next one, which starts a week before the current one ends, and the proxy switches to the next CA then on its own, without a launch. So a VM that you don’t open again keeps working for at least 30 days after its last launch with devvm in its folder. Connecting with ssh alone isn’t a launch. When a VM runs past its next CA’s end without a launch, its proxy refuses its HTTPS connections to secrets’ hosts, and devvm network log --blocked gives the reason devvm's CA has ended. The VM’s other requests keep working. Run devvm in the VM’s folder to install new CAs, which also starts the VM’s proxy again and ends the connections open through it (how). devvm rm deletes a VM’s CAs with the VM, and a VM keeps them when its tier changes.

devvm secret unuse and devvm secret rm take a secret away from a VM at once, because the VM only ever had its placeholder. Neither command revokes what a VM made with the secret (minting credentials with a secret), so rotate it if that matters. Use a fine-grained GitHub token, scoped to the repos your VMs need.

devvm secret –json

devvm secret --json prints the list as one JSON object, as output for scripts describes. Each of the secrets has its name, saved, which is true when it’s saved or, for claude, in devvm’s environment, and used_by, the names of the VMs using it. The JSON never holds a secret’s value.

{
 "version": 1,
 "secrets": [
 {
 "name": "claude",
 "saved": true,
 "used_by": [
 "devvm-some-project-71a99b1076d92c"
 ]
 },
 {
 "name": "github",
 "saved": false,
 "used_by": []
 },
 {
 "name": "proxy",
 "saved": false,
 "used_by": []
 }
 ]
}

Logs

devvm network log shows the proxy’s decisions for this folder’s VM, oldest first, one line each. A line has the time, allowed, BLOCKED or cache, and the host and port. An allowed line then has the rule that allowed it (, decrypted for an intercepted tunnel), the request (GET /user) and the secrets put in (, token: github), a blocked line has why it was blocked, and a cache line, a request to the shared Nix cache, has the request and what came of it:

2026-10-09T10:00:00Z BLOCKED example.com:443 not on the allowlist
2026-10-09T10:00:05Z allowed github.com:443 rule github.com
2026-10-09T10:00:06Z allowed api.github.com:443 GET /user, token: github
2026-10-09T10:00:07Z cache cache.nixos.org:443 GET /nix/yv1zf3y6all4j99aad30cb8i55dw9zmp.narinfo: hit
-n N, --lines N the last N (default 50)
--follow then each new one as it happens, until Ctrl+C
--blocked the blocks instead, one row per host and port, by when last blocked: LAST, COUNT, HOST and ALLOW WITH, the devvm network allow command that allows it

ALLOW WITH is - for a request that the proxy refuses whatever the allowlist says, such as a GitHub call that makes a credential, and for a host that isn’t a host name or an address. An open VM’s log holds what went through its proxy and its links’ connections, but not what the VM reached directly, and devvm network log says so. The proxy keeps each VM’s log to its last 10 to 20 MiB by starting a new file once the current one reaches 10 MiB and keeping one older file, which devvm network log reads too. devvm rm deletes the VM’s logs, and How it works describes the files.

devvm network log –json

devvm network log --json prints the last N events as one JSON object, as output for scripts describes, and devvm refuses it with --follow. Each of the events has what the proxy logged, without the VM’s name. That’s the time, the event, the host and the port, and, when the event has them, the request’s method and path, the rule that allowed it, the reason it was blocked or what came of a cache request, the request’s User-Agent header as agent, the secrets put in, refused for a request refused whatever the allowlist says, the company proxy it went through as upstream, and the VM that a link’s connection went to as target. The event is tunnel for an allowed connection, intercept for an allowed tunnel that the proxy decrypted, forward for an allowed request, blocked, or nix-cache for a request to the shared Nix cache. A link’s connection is link when devvm carried it, and link_refused, link_target_stopped or link_limit when devvm refused it, with the link’s name as its host. A log with nothing in it gives "events": [].

{
 "version": 1,
 "events": [
 {
 "time": "2026-10-09T10:00:00Z",
 "event": "blocked",
 "host": "example.com",
 "port": 443,
 "method": "CONNECT",
 "reason": "not on the allowlist"
 },
 {
 "time": "2026-10-09T10:00:06Z",
 "event": "forward",
 "host": "api.github.com",
 "port": 443,
 "method": "GET",
 "path": "/user",
 "secrets": [
 "github"
 ]
 }
 ]
}

With --blocked, each of the blocked has the last time it was blocked, the count, the host and the port, and allow, the rule that devvm network allow takes to allow it. A block that ALLOW WITH shows as - has no allow.

{
 "version": 1,
 "blocked": [
 {
 "last": "2026-10-09T10:01:00Z",
 "count": 2,
 "host": "example.com",
 "port": 443,
 "allow": "example.com"
 }
 ]
}

Links between VMs

A link between VMs lets a program in one VM, the client, reach a port that another VM, the target, publishes. devvm carries a link’s connections over ssh through this machine, so they use neither VM’s network, and a confined VM reaches only what its tier allows and the links you added to it. A client’s proxy is a second way into its links: it carries a request for one of the client’s own links, by the link’s name and port, to the same link on this machine, and passes it on as it is, without looking into it or putting a secret into it. It reaches no other socket on this machine and no other VM’s links. The allowlist’s rules don’t apply to links, so devvm network deny doesn’t stop one, and devvm link rm does.

A link joins the two VMs’ trust. Code in the client can often run code in the target through the target’s service, such as Postgres’s COPY … TO PROGRAM, and it then has whatever the target has: its network, the secrets it may use and its project folder. So devvm keeps two rules:

  • A client links only to a target on its own tier or a stricter one. An allowlist client links to allowlist and none targets, but not to internet or open ones, because a link to a target on a lower tier would let the client reach more through the target, around its own proxy. devvm checks this when you add a link, at each launch of the client and on every connection, and for a client on a confined tier, on every connection the target’s tier must be in force as it runs, so devvm refuses the connection while the target shows as unenforced, and it warns you of such a target when you add the link, when you publish a port in its folder that the client links to, and when the client starts. While such a link exists, devvm refuses to give the target a tier lower than the client’s, such as devvm network open, and it refuses to give the client a tier higher than a target’s, such as devvm network allowlist for a client that links to an open target. An open client may link to any target, and it then has the target’s secrets and project folder within reach as well as its own network.
  • The target publishes. A link reaches only a port that the target’s folder publishes with devvm link publish, and only on the target’s own loopback. Publishing offers the port to any of your VMs, and each link is still added in the client’s folder, so a VM reaches another’s service only when you’ve run a command in both folders.

The first rule keeps a client’s tier whole, but it doesn’t keep the target’s data in the target. A client on a confined tier can read whatever the target’s service gives it and send that out through the hosts its own tier reaches. Link two VMs only when you’d trust each with what the other has.

A group links each of its VMs to the ports that the others publish, once you’ve run devvm group join in each VM’s folder. Its VMs are all on one tier, so every link it makes keeps the first rule, and devvm refuses to change a VM’s tier with devvm network while it’s in a group. A group joins the trust of all its VMs, so put VMs in one only when you’d trust each with what the others have.

Not covered

The tiers leave some things open, such as what an allowed host accepts, whatever your secrets allow, such as pushes and API calls, and what a company CA that you add can read. Attack vectors lists them under Narrowed, not closed and Left to you.

item.title: .git protection
item.description:
The project folder is read-write in the VM, so without protection anything in the VM could add a git hook, or set core.fsmonitor, core.hooksPath or core.sshCommand in .git/config, and your next git command on this machine would run it. On macOS, devvm locks the git hooks and config with a flag that even root in the VM can’t clear, so nothing the VM does runs through them on this machine.

Every new VM gets .git protection. --no-git-protect creates a VM without it, and devvm git-protect changes it later. How it works › .git protection lists what devvm locks and when it checks the locks again.

What still works

git in the VM can commit, branch, check out, stash, fetch and pull, and git worktree add works on this machine. Commands that write .git/config fail with Operation not permitted, in the VM and on this machine. Those are git config, git remote add, push -u to a new branch, and hook installers such as husky or pre-commit. git worktree remove and prune also fail for the worktrees that were there when devvm locked .git.

To run them, stop the VM, unlock .git, run the commands on this machine, and lock it again:

devvm stop
devvm git-protect off
git config …
devvm git-protect on

Turning it on or off

devvm git-protect shows the VM’s protection, which is on, strict, off, or clone for a --clone VM, which mounts no .git. devvm git-protect on, strict or off changes it at once when the VM is stopped. A running VM could race the locks, so for a running VM devvm saves your choice and asks in a terminal whether to restart the VM now, which stops anything running in it. If you answer no, or there’s no terminal, or you pass --no-input, devvm says it saved the choice. It applies the choice the next time it finds the VM stopped: at the restart you agreed to, at devvm stop, at devvm restart, or, when the VM was stopped some other way, at the next launch, before the VM starts. Until then, devvm git-protect shows the protection the VM has, and a later choice replaces the saved one. Launches lock only a stopped VM for the same reason.

  • on locks .git as it is now and takes it as yours, so a .git that was replaced since the last lock isn’t reported, and the next launches compare with this one. It reports what a lock can’t stop and what’s not covered, as devvm did when it made the VM. If the folder has no .git yet, devvm locks it on the first launch after one appears.
  • strict is on plus strict.
  • off takes the locks off. The VM can then change .git hooks and config, which run on your machine.

On an existing VM, devvm ignores --no-git-protect and warns you. A --clone VM’s protection can’t be changed. devvm clone on takes the locks off once it has made the VM again with its own clone, and devvm clone off makes it mount the folder again with protection as a new VM gets it (switching a VM that exists).

devvm git-protect –json

devvm git-protect --json prints the VM’s protection as one JSON object with mode, which is on, strict, off or clone, as output for scripts describes. With --json the command only shows, so devvm refuses on, strict or off with it.

{
 "version": 1,
 "mode": "on"
}

Strict

The VM can add a submodule at any time, and git status and git diff on this machine read the submodule’s config. So the submodule’s core.fsmonitor would run on this machine before the VM’s next launch locks it. devvm git-protect strict closes that gap by setting diff.ignoreSubmodules = all in the locked .git/config. git status and git diff on this machine then never look inside submodules, and they don’t show the submodules’ changes. git submodule … and --recurse-submodules still enter them, so for a repo with submodules you don’t trust, use --clone.

devvm git-protect on and off take diff.ignoreSubmodules back out.

When devvm reports .git

Every launch of an existing VM, and devvm stop, check .git again, and devvm reports what it finds there that it didn’t lock. When it names one of these, check it before you run git in the folder, because git on this machine would run what the VM put there:

  • A repo that appeared in the folder after its VM was made. devvm locks it from then on, but if you didn’t make it, check its hooks and config.
  • Hooks in a folder devvm hadn’t locked, because the folder wasn’t there to lock or belongs to a new submodule.
  • A submodule whose git folder isn’t one. The VM can name any folder in the project as a submodule’s git folder, such as your src, so devvm locks nothing in a folder that doesn’t look like a git folder, and names the submodule instead.
  • A path that’s a symlink or under one. devvm never locks anything through a symlink, because the VM could point one at a file elsewhere on this machine, so it leaves that path unlocked.
  • A path that moved while devvm locked it. devvm leaves it unlocked and takes the lock off wherever it landed, so check .git.

How it works › .git protection lists every check.

Not covered

The lock covers .git, and the VM can still put things elsewhere that git on this machine runs. devvm tells you about each of these, so read what it reports before you run git in the folder, and use --clone for a repo you don’t trust.

  • Hooks in the working tree, such as husky’s .husky/ with core.hooksPath=.husky, or an absolute path into the project folder. The VM can edit them, and they run on this machine. devvm warns about them when it creates the VM.
  • What the locked files hand over to the project folder, which is an include.path or includeIf.*.path that leads into it, or a hook that’s a symlink into it. The VM can edit those files, and git on this machine reads or runs them. devvm warns about them when it creates the VM, and on a launch after they change.
  • Submodules whose git folder is outside the project. devvm can’t lock that folder, because another project’s VM may write it, and git status on this machine reads its config. devvm names these submodules when it creates the VM.
  • A replaced .git. The VM can rename .git and put a new one in its place, or point git at another config. devvm reports this on each launch but doesn’t undo it (what a lock can’t stop).

Linux hosts

Linux has no immutable flag that a user can set, so VMs on Linux hosts have no .git protection, and the VM can change .git hooks and config, which run on the host. devvm refuses devvm git-protect on and strict there, and --clone keeps the VM out of .git instead, so use it for any repo where you don’t trust what runs in the VM.

The warning at each launch

Each launch of a VM that mounts a folder with a .git warns that the VM can change its hooks and config, which run on this machine. That includes the launch that creates the VM, and launches of a VM that’s already running. Once you’ve read the warning and decided to go on without protection, run devvm git-protect off in the folder. devvm records that you chose it and stops warning for that VM, but it still names the changes that the next section describes. A VM that you create with --no-git-protect doesn’t warn either, and a --clone VM never warns, because it mounts no .git.

When devvm names a change

devvm can’t stop the VM from changing .git on a Linux host, but it notices the change afterwards. When devvm creates a VM, it records a hash of each path that a lock would cover on macOS, which are the hooks in .git/hooks, .git/config and the rest of what’s locked, submodules’ included. It also hashes .git/commondir, whether it’s there or not, and what the config hands over to the project folder: the files that an include.path leads to, and the hooks folder that core.hooksPath names, such as husky’s .husky. Each launch that finds the VM stopped, and devvm stop, hash them again and name every path that changed since the last check, such as .git/config and .git/hooks/pre-commit. A warning names ten paths at most, and then how many more changed. The same checks report what a lock can’t stop either, as they do on macOS: a .git that was replaced, a commondir, a repo or submodule that appeared, and includes, hook links and a core.hooksPath into the project folder (not covered). A launch of a VM that’s already running checks nothing, so run devvm stop when you want the check. A VM that devvm has no hashes for yet, such as one that an older devvm made, records them at its first check and names nothing.

devvm names a change only after it happened, so git on this machine may already have run a changed hook or read a changed config. devvm can’t tell who made a change, so it also names your own, such as a git remote add or git push -u that you ran on this machine. When it names a path that you didn’t change, check it before you run git in the folder:

  • git config --list --show-origin shows each setting of the repo and the file it comes from. Look for settings that run a program, such as core.fsmonitor, core.hooksPath, core.sshCommand, core.pager, filter.* and include.path.
  • ls -la .git/hooks lists the hooks, and git runs a hook there by its name, such as pre-commit, so read every file whose name doesn’t end in .sample.

If you find something that you didn’t put there, remove it, and use --clone for that repo.

What the watch can’t see

The watch isn’t a security boundary, and it doesn’t stop anything. It compares what’s in .git when the VM is stopped with what was there at the last check, so it misses a change that the VM made and then undid before it stopped, even though git on this machine may have run the change in between. It also can’t fully watch some paths, and it names them at every check until they’re gone:

  • A symlink, or a path under one, such as a hook that’s a symlink, or a .git that’s a symlink. devvm never follows a symlink out of the project folder, so it can’t see changes to what such a link points to. For a link that stays inside the project folder, it hashes what the link leads to as well.
  • A file larger than 16 MiB, which devvm records by its size, inode and change time, so it notices a change that keeps the size but can’t hash the file.
  • A hooks folder with more than 1,000 entries, which devvm records by its count and change time. It always hashes the hooks that git runs, at the folder’s top, before the rest.
  • What’s past 2,000 paths in all, across every git folder and hooks folder of the repo.

A repo rarely has any of these, so when devvm names one that you didn’t make, check what it holds, and use --clone for that repo.

item.title: Attack vectors
item.description:
This page lists the common ways that code you didn’t write gets to run on a developer’s machine or gets data off it, and what devvm does about each one. devvm stops most of them on its own, and the habits close most of what’s left. Narrowed, not closed and Left to you are the one list of what devvm leaves open, and each entry links to the page that explains its mechanism.

How devvm handles each attack

The rest of this page sorts the attacks by how much of each one devvm stops:
Blocked The attack can’t work, because what it’s after isn’t in the VM or the VM can’t reach it.
Kept inside the VM The attacker’s code runs, but it runs in the VM, where it reaches only the project folder and what you gave the VM.
Narrowed, not closed devvm closes part of the attack, and the entry says what’s still open.
Left to you devvm doesn’t stop the attack, and the entry says what to do instead.

Some protections hold only on some network tiers or only on macOS, and each entry names its conditions. Everything here rests on the VM’s boundary. How devvm does each of these is in the security model.

Blocked

Credentials on this machine

  • SSH keys. Malware on a developer’s machine looks in ~/.ssh first, because a private key opens every server and repo that trusts it. A VM never mounts ~/.ssh or anything else from your home folder, so there’s no key in it to copy. Agent forwarding, which you turn on yourself, lets the VM use your keys but never copy them.
  • Cloud, cluster and registry logins. Worms that steal credentials collect ~/.aws, ~/.config/gcloud, ~/.azure, ~/.kube/config, ~/.docker/config.json and the npm publish token in ~/.npmrc. A VM mounts none of them, so a package that goes looking finds nothing. Secrets you keep in the project folder are a different case, which Left to you covers.
  • The Keychain, browsers and password managers. Stealers read saved passwords, cookies and login sessions from browser profiles and the Keychain. The VM has no browser profile of yours, and it can’t reach this machine’s Keychain.
  • Your coding agents’ history. Agent transcripts hold what you pasted into them, such as secrets and code from other projects. Your history never goes into a VM, and each VM’s own history stays in that VM (coding agents).
  • Secrets, on every tier. Every VM, an open one included, gets a placeholder instead of each secret, such as your GitHub token or Claude Code’s token, and the proxy on this machine puts the real value only into requests for that secret’s own hosts (secrets). A placeholder copied out of the VM is worthless elsewhere, because it ends in a random value of that VM’s own, and an open VM that sends a request around its proxy sends only the placeholder. Another VM or a program on this machine can’t spend the secret through the proxy either, because the proxy needs the VM’s own password. Codex and opencode logins and Claude Code’s MCP secrets work the same way, and devvm refreshes OAuth logins on this machine, so a VM never holds a refresh token.

Git running code on this machine

  • Git hooks and config, on macOS. A VM can write the project folder, so without protection it could add a hook such as .git/hooks/post-checkout, or set a command in .git/config: core.fsmonitor, core.hooksPath, core.sshCommand, core.pager, core.editor, a filter.* or diff.*.textconv driver, a credential.helper or a ! alias. Your next git command on this machine would run it. devvm locks hooks and config with a flag that even root in the VM can’t clear (.git protection). Linux hosts have no such flag, which Left to you covers.
  • The shell prompt. Many shell prompts and editors run git status as soon as you cd into a folder or open it, and git status runs core.fsmonitor. The lock covers that as well, so opening the folder runs nothing that the VM wrote into .git.
  • devvm’s own git commands. devvm runs git on this machine itself, for example to read your name and email for the VM, to check a --clone VM’s repo for uncommitted changes, and to fetch from the VM. A VM can write a repo that git on this machine reads, such as the project folder’s on Linux or a repo inside a folder it mounts, so devvm’s git runs none of the programs a repo’s config can name. It turns off the repo’s fsmonitor, its hooks, including those its config defines, and its filters, it never enters a submodule for git status, and it uses no transport but ssh, so git status, a fetch or a push of devvm’s runs nothing that the VM wrote into the repo. It ignores the git variables of the shell you run devvm in, such as GIT_DIR and GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL, so it never works on another repo or config by mistake, and it never asks you anything (GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0). Its fetches and pushes reach the VM with ssh in batch mode (-o BatchMode=yes), so the VM’s ssh server can’t ask you for a password. They always connect to that VM itself, whatever host the repo’s config sends them to, accept only the host key devvm pinned for it, and forward neither your agent nor any port.

Getting out over the network, on the allowlist and none tiers

  • Sending data to the attacker’s server. Most attacks end by sending what they stole to a server the attacker runs. A confined VM reaches only its proxy, and on the allowlist tier the proxy allows only the hosts on the VM’s allowlist, and on the none tier only its agents’ and secrets’ hosts. On the internet tier the proxy allows every public host, the attacker’s included, so this holds only for this machine and your networks. devvm leaves storage and paste sites out of the default allowlist on purpose, because they’re easy ways to send data out (allowlists).
  • DNS tunnelling. An attacker can encode data into names and look them up at a DNS server of their own. A VM sends no DNS queries of its own, because names resolve in the proxy on this machine.
  • Services on this machine and your network. Code in a VM could attack what developers leave open on localhost, such as databases, dev servers, Docker’s API and other VMs’ ports. It could also attack your router, a NAS, or a cloud provider’s metadata service at 169.254.169.254. The proxy refuses this machine’s own addresses and internal ones, such as loopback, private, link-local and CGNAT ranges, unless a rule names the address (the proxy).
  • DNS rebinding and address tricks. A name can resolve to a public address when it’s checked and to an internal one when it’s dialed, and an internal address can hide in an IPv6 or NAT64 form. The proxy dials only the address it checked, and it sees through NAT64 forms (the proxy).
  • Going around the proxy. Root in a VM can change its routes and firewall, but devvm confines the VM from outside it, so nothing in the VM reaches anything but the proxy (confinement). devvm catches a VM started outside devvm, or one given a second network, with the self-check. It stops a VM that gets out through a second network, and it offers to restart one started outside devvm confined, or stops it when there’s no terminal to ask in.

Spreading beyond the VM

  • Your agents’ config. A rogue agent could add a hook to ~/.claude/settings.json or a skill to ~/.claude/skills, so that it runs the next time you use the agent on this machine. devvm mounts the agents’ config folders read-only, which this machine enforces, and copies their files in on every launch, so nothing the VM changes goes back (mounts). Only devvm agent save copies a VM’s settings into devvm’s agent store, for every VM, and it shows what changed and asks first, so read its diff for hooks, MCP servers and plugins you didn’t add (saving a VM’s settings).
  • Other projects and other VMs. Each project folder gets its own VM with its own disk, and a VM mounts only its own project folder. Each VM’s proxy has its own password, so one VM can’t use another’s secrets. A VM reaches a service in another VM only through a link between VMs that you add in its folder, to a port that the other VM’s folder publishes. A link joins the two VMs’ trust, because code in one can often run code in the other through its service, so a VM links only to a VM on its own tier or a stricter one, and nothing in a VM can add a link (links between VMs).
  • Images, layers and devvm itself. Malware could try to make itself permanent by editing an image, a layer script or devvm’s own files. devvm builds images with nothing from this machine mounted, and the shared tools are read-only in every VM. devvm also refuses a project folder that holds its own folders or sits inside them, so a VM can’t reach the layer scripts that every build runs or the files devvm runs on this machine (only the project folder).
  • A folder made again. If you delete a repo and clone another at the same path, the new folder never gets the old VM’s disk or anything left in it. devvm knows a folder by its inode as well as its path, so it refuses and offers devvm rm or devvm adopt (a folder made again).
  • A devcontainer.json that reaches this machine. Other tools run a devcontainer’s initializeCommand on the host. devvm never runs it, refuses ${localEnv:…}, adds no mounts from the file and doesn’t follow a link out of the folder (devcontainer.json). devvm uses the file’s image only when the image’s registry gives it to anyone who asks, and it refuses a registry on this machine or its network. Behind a company proxy, devvm looks the image up through the company proxy and checks only the registry’s name, so a company proxy that reaches this machine or its network for a name that looks public takes the lookup there (the design note).
  • Impersonating a VM. ssh checks a VM against host keys that devvm reads through the VM’s backend instead of over the network, so a program that answers on the VM’s port in its place is refused (ssh access by name).

Kept inside the VM

The attacks in this section run the attacker’s code, and devvm doesn’t stop that code from running. It runs in the VM, as the VM’s user, who has passwordless sudo. From there it reaches the project folder, or with --clone the VM’s own clone of it, and the secrets the VM uses, which are placeholders on every tier. It reaches what the VM’s tier allows: the hosts on the allowlist on the allowlist tier, every public host on the internet tier, and the whole network on the open tier. Everything in Blocked still holds. What the code writes into the project folder can still reach you when a program on this machine runs it, which Left to you covers.

Install and build scripts

  • npm, yarn, pnpm and bun lifecycle scripts. A package’s preinstall, install, postinstall and prepare scripts run any command when the package is installed, and most npm attacks use them. pnpm’s build approvals (pnpm approve-builds) and --ignore-scripts narrow which packages run scripts, and they’re still worth using, but a package you approved runs its scripts all the same, even one compromised after you approved it. In a VM, those scripts reach only what this section’s introduction lists.
  • Python packages. Installing a source distribution runs its setup.py or its build backend, and a .pth file in site-packages runs code every time Python starts.
  • Ruby gems. A gem with a native extension runs its extconf.rb when it’s installed, and Bundler can install gems straight from a git repo.
  • Rust build scripts and procedural macros. build.rs and procedural macros run on cargo build and cargo check, and also when rust-analyzer opens the project, so opening the folder in an editor is enough to run them. With devvm code, VS Code’s extensions, rust-analyzer among them, run in the VM (devvm host and devvm code).
  • Go modules. Go has no install scripts, but cgo passes flags to the C compiler, go generate runs commands, a toolchain line in go.mod makes Go download another toolchain, and a module’s init functions run in every test and program that imports it.
  • Makefiles, task runners and curl | sh. A Makefile, a justfile or a project’s install line from its README runs whatever its author wrote.

Bad packages and images

  • Typosquatting, dependency confusion and made-up names. Attackers publish packages under names one typo away from popular ones, under a company’s internal package names with a higher version, and under names that AI coding agents invent and that attackers then register. Their code runs as the scripts above do.
  • Compromised maintainers. A trusted package can turn malicious when its maintainer’s account is taken over or a new maintainer joins with bad intent, as event-stream (2018) and xz (2024) did. Updating such a package runs its new code in the VM.
  • Malicious images. An image from --from or from a devcontainer’s image runs its own code as root in the build VM (the image is untrusted). devvm uses only images that the registry gives to anyone who asks anonymously, never one that only your Docker or your registry login reaches, and it confines builds so they reach the internet but not this machine’s services (read-only and confined builds).
  • A devcontainer.json’s commands and features. A project’s postCreateCommand and its other commands run in the VM as the VM’s user, as soon as devvm makes the VM. Its image and features decide what’s in the VM, and devvm adds its ports to the ones it forwards to this machine’s localhost, even beyond a list you narrowed, so the VM is the project’s from the start. Its features can only be devvm’s own layers, so devvm never fetches or runs a feature’s script. devvm --no-devcontainer skips the file for a project you don’t trust that far (devcontainer.json).

Rogue agents

  • Prompt injection. Instructions hidden in a README, an issue, a code comment, a web page, a dependency’s docs or an MCP tool’s output can turn a coding agent against you. devvm can’t tell an agent’s own work from injected work, so it limits what the agent reaches instead. An attack like this needs private data, untrusted input and a way to send the data out. On the allowlist tier, the only way out is the hosts on the allowlist, which Left to you covers.
  • Agents with their checks off. An agent run with claude --dangerously-skip-permissions or codex --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox acts without asking, and a mistaken rm -rf ~ or sudo command reaches only the VM. The project folder is still the agent’s to change, so commit often, or use --clone to keep the agent’s work apart until you fetch it.
  • Malware that stays. Anything the attacker leaves in the VM, such as a cron job, a changed shell startup file or a backdoored program, stays in that VM and goes into no other, unless you save an agent’s settings that it changed with devvm agent save. devvm never deletes a VM on its own, because it may hold unsaved work, so save what you need and run devvm rm, then make the VM again.
  • Mining and resource abuse. A VM’s CPUs, memory and disk are capped by its size, which devvm size shows and changes (size). The VM’s proxy on this machine carries at most 1024 tunnels for it at once, but it doesn’t count the VM’s plain HTTP requests in absolute form or its idle kept-alive connections (the proxy).

Narrowed, not closed

Secrets and keys the VM may use

  • Worms that use your GitHub token. Shai-Hulud (2025) spread through npm install scripts. It collected npm, GitHub and cloud credentials, then used them to publish repos and new versions of packages. A VM holds no npm or cloud credentials, and its GitHub token is a placeholder. The proxy still puts the real GitHub token into every request to GitHub’s hosts, so a worm in the VM can push, make repos and do whatever else the GitHub token’s scope allows. Use a fine-grained GitHub token scoped to the repos the VM needs, or bind none (saving and binding secrets).
  • Minting credentials with a secret. A VM that can use a secret can use it to make another credential that outlasts it. The proxy refuses GitHub REST calls that add an SSH key, a deploy key, a self-hosted runner or a webhook with 403, but it can’t refuse everything, such as GitHub’s GraphQL API, an OAuth app grant or other services. A bound API key can make credentials too. With Google Gemini’s key, code in the VM can ask generativelanguage.googleapis.com for an ephemeral token for Gemini’s Live API, which lasts up to about 20 hours and allows as many uses as the VM asks for. With xAI’s key it can ask api.x.ai for a realtime client secret that lasts as long as the VM chooses, and with OpenAI’s key it can ask api.openai.com for one that lasts up to 2 hours. These credentials work without the proxy, and the proxy allows the requests that make them, because opencode’s experimental voice mode makes them itself (API keys the proxy puts in). If a VM may have done this, rotate the secret and check the service’s keys, access tokens and runners.
  • Keys devvm can’t tell apart. devvm takes the keys out of the VM’s copies of your agents’ settings and logins only where it can tell a key from the rest. A key in other text, such as a hook’s command, stays when it neither starts like a known key nor follows Bearer or Basic. The entries of Codex’s login that devvm doesn’t know go in as they are, and devvm names each one. opencode’s and pi’s keys that devvm can’t bind, such as a local model server’s, stay on this machine unless you list their provider in config.toml’s [pass-keys], and then they go in as they are. The agents’ folders that the VM mounts whole, such as ~/.claude/skills or ~/.config/opencode/plugin, reach the VM with every file in them, so a .env in one is in the VM, and so is a private plugin marketplace’s git config with a password or an access token in its URL. Keep secrets out of those folders (what stays in the VM’s copies).
  • Your SSH agent. While agent forwarding is on, anything in the VM can use the agent’s keys to push or log in to servers, though it can’t copy them. The VM has the agent while you’re connected. devvm ssh-agent devvm limits it to the keys you add to devvm’s own agent, and an agent that asks you to approve each use, such as 1Password’s or Secretive, narrows it further.

Git

  • Submodules with their own config. The VM writes .git/index to commit, so it can add a submodule whose config sets core.fsmonitor. Host git status reads that config before devvm’s next launch finds the submodule and locks it. devvm git-protect strict stops git status and git diff from looking inside submodules, but git submodule commands still enter them, so use --clone for a repo with submodules you don’t trust.
  • Replacing .git. The VM can rename .git and put a new one in its place, or add a commondir that points git at another config. devvm reports these on each launch but doesn’t prevent them, so check what it names before you run git in the folder (what a lock can’t stop).

Network

  • Domain fronting. The proxy checks the host name that a TLS connection asks for, its SNI, but not the Host inside the encrypted traffic, so a CDN that serves many sites on one address can route an allowed connection to a site that isn’t allowed. The proxy reads the connections to hosts with a bound secret, and it refuses a request in them that names another host.
  • Model providers that fetch for the VM. The proxy allows a bound API key’s provider hosts on port 443, and some providers’ own tools fetch URLs that the request names, such as Google Gemini’s URL context and Search grounding, xAI’s live search, Groq’s compound models and Mistral’s agents with web search, as Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s web fetch and search tools do. Code in the VM can send data out through such a tool to a host that the allowlist doesn’t have (API keys the proxy puts in).
  • Ports the VM listens on. devvm forwards the VM’s TCP ports from 1024 up to this machine’s localhost, unless you list the ports with --ports, so a VM could take a port that a program on this machine trusts while that port is free, and what the VM serves there reaches whatever connects to it. devvm’s forwarder never takes a port that a program on this machine already has, or one that devvm records for a VM, but a program that binds a port on all addresses after devvm forwarded it gets its localhost connections sent to the VM. devvm ports limits what a VM forwards, and devvm ports none forwards nothing, though a project’s devcontainer.json adds its forwardPorts to that list when devvm makes the VM or devvm update reads the file (devcontainer.json, ports, port forwarding).
  • VS Code’s relays. Over Remote-SSH, which devvm code opens, VS Code forwards the ports that programs in the VM listen on, and it answers git’s prompts with your GitHub sign-in. devvm turns both off in the VM’s VS Code settings each time it sets the VM up, but the VM can turn them back on, so turn them off in your own VS Code settings as well (VS Code).
  • What a VM does through a link. A link between VMs joins the two VMs’ trust. Code in the client can often run code in the target through the service it reaches, such as Postgres’s COPY … TO PROGRAM, and it then has the target’s network, the secrets it may use and its project folder. devvm limits a link to the ports the target publishes, on the target’s loopback, and a client to targets on its own tier or a stricter one, but it doesn’t limit what the service does. In a group, every VM trusts every other in the same way, and a VM that joins later gets the same reach (links between VMs).
  • History imported from a less strict tier. An export of agents’ history carries what the old VM’s agents read, so importing one from an open VM into a VM on the allowlist tier can bring in credentials and data that the new VM couldn’t reach itself, along with any instructions planted in them. devvm warns before such an import, and before importing an export whose tier it has no record of, but it imports all the same. Import history only from a VM you trusted as much as the new one (importing history).
  • What one VM learns of another through the shared Nix cache. VMs with the nix layer share one cache of Nix’s packages on this machine. A VM can tell by how fast the cache answers whether some VM fetched a public package. The packages are public, and a project’s flake.lock names the ones it needs, so this tells a VM only that another project on this machine uses a package. A VM that fetches many packages can also fill the cache up to its cap and push other VMs’ packages out, so they download them again, but it can’t fill the disk past the cap or keep anything that cache.nixos.org didn’t sign (the shared Nix cache).
  • Through a company proxy. The company proxy looks up the names it’s sent itself, and it may get another answer than this machine did, or a later one, so the VM’s proxy can’t check every address a name leads to there. Under a name that an allowlist names, a VM reaches whatever the company proxy reaches, such as your company’s internal hosts and the company proxy’s own host, which is this machine’s loopback when the company proxy runs on this machine, as a VPN client’s does. A name that the VM’s allowlist doesn’t allow never reaches the company proxy (the design note).
  • Which names resolve to internal addresses. When the proxy refuses a name because this machine’s lookup gives it an internal address, its refusal says so, so a VM can learn which names this machine’s DNS resolves to internal addresses. The refusal never names the address, this machine’s DNS server or the company proxy, which stay in the proxy’s own log (log files).

This machine

  • A nested project replaced through its parent folder’s VM. A project with a VM of its own inside a folder with another VM is in both VMs, so code in the parent folder’s VM can replace the nested project folder with a link, such as one to your home folder, which the nested VM would mount at its next start. devvm warns each time it makes or opens such a nested VM, naming the parent folder’s VM. It checks the nested folder, by its path and by the folder itself, just before it starts the nested VM and again once the VM runs, and it refuses the start or stops the VM again when the folder was replaced. On macOS the VM mounts the folder itself rather than its path, so it never mounts what a link points to, even when the folder is put back before devvm checks again. On Linux the VM mounts the folder by its path, so code that replaces the folder for the moment the VM’s backend mounts it and puts it back before devvm checks again stays unseen, and the VM keeps what the link pointed to until its next start. Keep a nested project that you don’t want the parent folder’s VM to reach out of the parent folder (a nested project replaced).
  • Set-id files on Linux hosts. Root in a VM can set the set-user-id bit on a file in the project folder, and on Linux hosts that bit reaches the host, so the file runs as its owner for whoever runs it. devvm names such files when it makes a VM and once a VM is stopped, but not at a launch into a running VM, and Troubleshooting says how to clear them. Don’t run programs from the project folder outside the VM (set-id files).
  • The proxy’s CA keys. Inside a VM, its CA vouches for any site, so someone with a copy of its key and a place on your network could impersonate sites to that VM. Each VM has CAs of its own, so a copy reaches one VM and no other. Only you can read the keys, they never leave this machine, and devvm keeps them out of Time Machine. Each CA lasts 30 days, so a copy goes stale, but the next CA’s key is on disk for up to 23 days before that CA starts, so a copy of it taken then works until that CA ends, up to 53 days later. Keep ~/.local/share/devvm/vms out of other backup and sync tools as well, and on Linux, which has no Time Machine, out of your backups (the VM’s CA).
  • Your company proxy’s password. No VM gets the company proxy’s settings: an open VM goes through its own proxy, which goes through the company proxy for it. devvm keeps the password out of its run logs only where it can tell it’s a password, so one in an address with neither a scheme nor a port, one with a raw /, ?, # or @ in it, or one in a run of more than 4 KiB without a space that a command writes in pieces can stay. Lima’s own log for the VM holds the password until the VM has started, when devvm replaces it with as many *, so the log still shows its length. If devvm is killed before then, or you run limactl start outside devvm, the log keeps it. With config.toml’s proxy, the mise that devvm runs on this machine gets the password in its environment, where programs that run as you can read it (open VMs and builds, the run log).

Left to you

Files the VM writes

The VM can write anything in the project folder, and devvm locks only .git. Any other file there that a program on this machine runs, or reads as its config, is the VM’s to change. --clone keeps all of these away from this machine until you fetch the VM’s work and review it.

  • Hooks in the working tree. Hooks kept in the project, such as husky’s .husky/ with core.hooksPath pointing there, run on this machine, and so do an include.path or a hook symlink that leads into the folder. devvm warns about them when it makes the VM (not covered).
  • Agent config in the project. Claude Code reads a project’s .claude/settings.json, whose hooks run commands, and .mcp.json, which starts MCP servers, and agents follow a project’s CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md. pi reads a project’s .pi folder, whose extensions run as code when pi starts, whose settings.json installs packages and sets shellCommandPrefix, which comes before every command pi runs, and whose mcp.json starts MCP servers. pi asks before it loads them, unless your ~/.pi/agent/trust.json on this machine already trusts the folder or your settings trust every folder. Running an agent on this machine in the folder after the VM has worked in it runs what the VM wrote, so run your agents in the VM.
  • Editor and tool config. VS Code runs .vscode/tasks.json tasks set to runOn: folderOpen and starts the interpreters and formatters that .vscode/settings.json names. direnv loads .envrc, and mise reads mise.toml’s environment, hooks and tasks. Keep VS Code’s workspace trust on, and use direnv’s and mise’s own approval prompts.
  • Project code and binaries. npm install, make, a test run or ./bin/tool on this machine runs whatever the VM wrote. Run them in the VM instead.
  • Symlinks out of the folder. The VM can create a link in the project folder that points at a file of yours, such as ~/.ssh/id_ed25519. A program on this machine that follows it, such as an upload, an archive or an agent reading files, reads your file instead. devvm itself never follows a link out of the folder.
  • Backdoors in code you merge. Treat the VM’s commits as an untrusted contributor’s, and review them before you merge, deploy or publish them.
  • Secrets in the project folder. A .env file, a project .npmrc or a cloud key in the folder is in the VM. On the allowlist tier it can reach only the hosts on the allowlist, on the internet tier any public host, and on the open tier anywhere. Keep secrets out of the project folder, or use --clone, which copies no untracked files into the VM. The same goes for your agents’ config folders, which keys devvm can’t tell apart covers (mounts).

The network

  • Allowed hosts. Anything an allowed host accepts can carry data out. github.com accepts a push from anyone with an account, including an attacker with an account of their own, and the npm registry accepts packages the same way. Keep allowlists short, and check what a VM reached with devvm network log.
  • What your secrets allow. A VM can push with a GitHub token it may use and spend Claude quota. Use a fine-grained GitHub token, and bind only the secrets a VM needs.
  • Open VMs. An open VM, because you chose open or passed --network open, reaches everything this machine can, including its services on localhost, such as other VMs’ ports, dev servers and databases, and your local network, directly and through its proxy, which applies no rules for it. Its proxy still puts its secrets in, so it can spend them on their hosts as any VM can, but it holds only their placeholders, as every VM does. A VM started outside devvm, such as with limactl start, or one running since before devvm network gave it a confined tier, runs unconfined in the same way until devvm restarts it confined (the self-check).
  • Your browser. Programs in a VM can open URLs in this machine’s browser, and a page that a VM serves on a forwarded port runs in your browser like any other. From there it can reach the internet past the VM’s tier, and your services on localhost.
  • Remote forwards you add. A RemoteForward in your ssh config, or an ssh -R you type, makes this machine connect to whatever it names for the VM. devvm’s ssh entries can’t turn off a RemoteForward of yours without also refusing an ssh -R you type. The VM’s ssh server refuses a remote forward on any address outside 127.77.0.0/16, the range devvm keeps for links between VMs, so one on the VM’s localhost, which ssh -R asks for by default, is refused. Root in the VM can change that setting, though, and the server allows a forward on an address in 127.77.0.0/16 for anyone it lets in. A forward you ask for by a host name that begins with 127.77. binds whatever address that name resolves to in the VM. So keep remote forwards out of Host *, and don’t forward into a VM you don’t trust (ssh into VMs).
  • A company CA you add. A company CA that you put in ~/.config/devvm/ca can read the TLS traffic of every VM, whatever its tier, as it can this machine’s, and the proxy trusts it for its own connections. Only that folder adds CAs to the proxy, and nothing a VM sends can.

The platform

  • .git on Linux hosts. Linux has no flag a user can set to lock a file, so VMs on Linux hosts have no .git protection, and the VM can change hooks and config that run on the host. Use --clone there (Linux hosts).
  • Escaping the VM. A bug in Lima, Apple’s Virtualization framework or QEMU could let code out of the VM.
